## Bible sentences that favor or rule out an option
No sentence rules out A, B or C; the Fuse sheet frames all three as open proposals and explicitly withholds a pick: "No direction selects a final element pool, failure rate, instability meter or self-damage amount" (BIBLE.md:359). BACKLOG.md:2856 (Q-P04) confirms the construction choice is still an open decision reserved to Andrew.

Two sentences favor C on textual grounds: BIBLE.md:354 ("Swappable working chambers visibly support multiple elements while preserving a dependable aiming direction") and BIBLE.md:357/359 ("separate elemental outlets legible above an open cable frame") describe exactly the multi-element legibility § 5.1's landmark rule requires ("Fuse an aiming nozzle," "Attack previews and damage must use the same committed geometry," BIBLE.md:416). AD-11's "never hide the pilot, working mechanism or class silhouette beneath scrap noise" (BIBLE.md:682) is a generic caution that most directly names A's stacking risk, but it is not written as a rule-out of A specifically — labeled inference/caution only.

## Gaps and open items
- Q-P13 (BACKLOG.md:2978-2988) leaves pool, eligibility, frequency, severity and warning timing open — the miscast-legibility comparisons above (row 6) are structural inferences about each construction's *capacity* to localize a miscast, not settled design.
- Q-P32 (TRACKING.md:257) and PD-01 AC-10 (docs/product/sections/PD-01-art-acceptance.md:45) require "construction differs where behaviour differs" and a readable working tool per class — all three candidates satisfy this at the concept-sheet level per BIBLE.md:359; none has been checked against a gameplay camera distance (Q-P32's aim-point bounds remain open, TRACKING.md:257).
- Production-cost claims (mount points, reuse, procedural-motion fit) are inference under Andrew's hybrid approach; no source names an asset budget or rig plan for any Fuse variant.
- BIBLE.md:428's four paired studies (nozzle → shaped conductor jaws; field conductor → separated pole shoes) describe a generic Fuse-like emitter family, not A/B/C specifically — cited as supporting context, not as evidence for one construction over another.

results.plain_rationale: The Bible says Fuse's weapon must "visibly support multiple elements" through swappable chambers while keeping "a dependable aiming direction" (BIBLE.md:354), and C is the only construction whose own description is built around that idea: "separate elemental outlets legible above an open cable frame" (BIBLE.md:359). That open frame keeps the pilot and the aiming nozzle landmark (BIBLE.md:416) in view, which is what AD-11 demands (BIBLE.md:682), whereas A's tall stack is the one most likely to crowd the aim line and B's squat block tends to fold the nozzle into the body. When Fuse gains a new element or upgrade, C shows it as a new or changed head on the hoop, which passes the "can the player identify the hardware change" test (BIBLE.md:69) more directly than more canisters or a swapped module inside a workbench. For miscasts, a single head sparking on the hoop lets the player see instability before harm without touching the aimed nozzle's committed geometry, matching Andrew's recorded rule that a miscast never changes the previewed danger shape (TRACKING.md:238). Production cost is my inference only: repeated head mounts on one hoop fit a procedural rotate/swap motion better than a wobbling stack or bespoke workbench modules.
results.player_feel: The player sees a ring of distinct outlets around Fuse and reads at a glance which elements the mech carries and which one is armed; picking up a new element visibly adds or swaps a head, so the build grows in front of them. Aiming stays trustworthy because the nozzle direction never changes when a head misbehaves; a miscast reads as one head crackling, venting frost or shorting on the hoop before it bites, so the "Still technically worked" beat lands as a visible, local mishap rather than a whole-mech fizzle. Fuse feels like a clever apprentice juggling too many tools in plain sight, not a bomb waiting to go off (A) or a tidy appliance (B).
results.runner_up: A (pressure-canister stack). It has the strongest "precarious apprentice" characterization (BIBLE.md:346, 359) and canister count is a cheap, legible growth tell, but the vertical stack beside the aiming barrel (BIBLE.md:344) is the option most at risk of hiding the working mechanism or class silhouette (BIBLE.md:682) and of crowding the aim line at the close third-person camera (BIBLE.md:663). B is a distant third: the squat workbench is the safest for occlusion but gives the fewest distinct external slots for visible element changes, which weakens the Pillar 2 hardware-change test (BIBLE.md:69).
risks_to_watch: Camera occlusion at gameplay distance is untested for every option (Q-P32 open, TRACKING.md:257 per packet, not re-read this session); a hoop that rings the cockpit could still block the pilot or sightline if mounted too high or too close. Require a camera-distance silhouette check before the model is locked.

A ring of heads can read as decorative attachments if the heads are not shown as working mechanisms; AD-11 forbids upgrades reduced to cosmetic attachments (BIBLE.md:681). Each head needs a visible mechanism change (e.g. shaped conductor jaws, BIBLE.md:428), not a colour swap.

Miscast localization is a structural inference: Q-P13 leaves pool, eligibility, frequency, severity and warning timing open (TRACKING.md:238). C makes it easier to isolate a miscast to one head, but no design proves it yet.

Production-cost ranking is inference; no source names an asset budget or rig plan for any Fuse variant. Confirm with the engineering handoff that a shared hoop mount plus swappable head props actually fits the hybrid procedural/hand-keyed approach.
Andrew retains the product decision (BACKLOG.md:2856 per packet, not re-read this session); this is one opinion, not consensus, and BIBLE.md:359 explicitly withholds a pick.
